name: Exosome facial

lead: An exosome facial applies or injects a product marketed as containing exosomes, tiny vesicles released by cells, usually after microneedling or laser. People use it for smoother texture, fewer acne scars and better overall skin quality, and it is positioned as a next step beyond PRP.

Exosomes carry RNA and proteins between cells, and proponents say products from stem-cell or other sources signal skin cells to repair tissue and lift skin quality. Most supporting research is cell and animal work, and registered human studies are small, mostly 7 to 40 people.

paras: A clinic applies the product to skin opened up by microneedling or laser, or injects it, as a single session or short series. Source cells named for these products include stem cells, adipose tissue, umbilical cord and plants.

The FDA stated in 2019 that no exosome products were approved and reported serious adverse events in patients given unapproved exosome-labelled products in Nebraska. Product sources and quality vary between providers.

web.title: FDA Public Safety Notification on Exosome Products

angle.text: Exosome facials apply a cell-derived product after microneedling or laser to improve skin texture, scarring and overall quality by boosting the skin's repair signals. Human studies so far are small and early, and no exosome product is FDA-approved.

lead: An exosome facial is an aesthetic procedure in which a product marketed as containing exosomes, small membrane-enclosed vesicles released by cells, is applied to or introduced into the facial skin, commonly after microneedling or laser treatment, with the aim of improving skin quality, texture and scarring. [1][2] Exosomes are one subtype of extracellular vesicle, and the source cells for aesthetic products vary: mesenchymal stem cells, adipose tissue, umbilical cord, and plants have all been named in trial registrations. [3][4][5]

In looksmaxxing and aesthetic-clinic circles the treatment is positioned as a next-generation alternative to platelet-rich plasma and similar regenerative procedures. Published evidence is early: the entries found are small registered studies, many with 7 to 40 participants, and several are listed as completed without published results in the record reviewed. [6][7][8]

The US Food and Drug Administration stated in a 2019 public safety notification that no exosome products were FDA-approved, and reported serious adverse events in patients treated with unapproved exosome-labelled products in Nebraska. [9]

Stem-cell, adipose, umbilical cord or plant-derived vesicles

paras: Exosomes are vesicles formed inside cells and released when an internal compartment fuses with the cell membrane. Wikipedia's article on extracellular vesicles notes that the word has been used inconsistently and that 'extracellular vesicle' is the preferred term unless a particular origin has been shown. [10] Vesicles can carry RNA between cells, and much of the research on their regenerative or anti-aging potential comes from cell culture and animal models. [10]

In aesthetic practice, exosome products are described as being applied topically following a skin-penetrating step such as microneedling, radiofrequency microneedling or fractional laser, or injected into the skin. Registered studies describe combinations with microneedling devices, fractional CO2 laser, Q-switched laser, and subcision. [2][3][6][7][11]

A search of ClinicalTrials.gov finds a cluster of small, recent registrations. They include a 30-participant phase 4 study of topical exosomes applied with a microneedling device for facial skin aging (completed, started 2024) [2], a 20-participant phase 3 study combining laser and exosomes for skin rejuvenation (completed, started 2025) [11], and a 12-participant study of AnteAGE exosomes with microneedling for facial skin quality [12]. A 30-participant study examined AnteAGE biosomes with radiofrequency microneedling for rejuvenation, wrinkles and skin tone [7], and a 7-participant proof-of-concept study examined a secretome/exosome serum for cosmetic improvement [6].

Several registrations concern atrophic acne scars: a 12-participant pilot combining subcision, adipose-derived exosomes and powdered polydioxanone [4]; a 22-participant study of umbilical-cord and bone-marrow stem-cell-derived exosomes [8]; and a 30-participant study comparing fractional CO2 laser with plant-derived exosomes against non-cross-linked hyaluronic acid [5]. A 38-participant study observed exosomes after Q-switched laser surgery [3], and a 40-participant phase 3 study of intradermal stem-cell-derived exosomes on facial skin quality is registered as not yet recruiting. [1]

The registrations reviewed do not themselves report outcomes, and the studies are small. No large randomized controlled trial or systematic review of exosome facials was identified in the sources consulted.

In December 2019 the FDA stated that there were no FDA-approved exosome products, that exosomes used to treat diseases in humans are generally regulated as drugs and biological products requiring premarket review, and that some clinics offer exosome products outside that process. [9] The agency reported multiple serious adverse events among patients in Nebraska treated with unapproved products marketed as containing exosomes, and asked health professionals and consumers to report adverse events through MedWatch. [9]
The notice advises patients to ask whether the FDA has reviewed a treatment and to understand known risks before consenting. [9] Regulation elsewhere varies and was not examined here.

timeline.event: FDA issues a public safety notification stating no exosome products are approved and reporting serious adverse events in Nebraska. [9]
Start of a registered observational study of exosomes after Q-switched laser surgery. [3]
Start of registered studies of exosomes with microneedling and radiofrequency microneedling. [2][7]
Several small registered studies of exosomes with laser or microneedling begin. [11][12][8][5]
